newsitem.title: UK: Boeing rules out rejoining superjumbo race.
newsitem.headline: Boeing rules out rejoining superjumbo race.

text.p: Boeing Co was adamant on Monday that archrival Airbus Industrie is in a one-horse race to produce the first superjumbo airliner.

Boeing chairman and chief executive Phil Condit told Reuters that contrary to recent industry speculation the company was not preparing to surprise the market by launching a new large aircraft if Airbus goes ahead as planned with the launch of its 550-seat A3XX in two years time.

He said Boeing was not going to develop a superjumbo, having just decided to drop proposals to develop a $7 billion stretched version of its 747-400, which at 380-425 seats in three-class configuration is the largest airliner in service.

"I doubt it," he said in a brief interview. "We are clearly working on what other possibilities there are so that we know what they are," he said. But he did not envisage that Boeing would want to advance anything new in the superjumbo category in the next couple of years, he said, because he did not believe there was sufficient demand.

"This is not a game," he said, after making a speech to an American-British Chamber of Commerce industry dinner. "If it were to happen it would be because there was a major major shift in the market."
"The real issue is a market issue and our best judgement to date is that the market is limited and we cannot make a business case for doing it."
Instead the company would concentrate on marketing proposals for extending capacities and ranges within its existing product ranges, including the 757, the 767 and 777 twinjets, he said.

The world's largest commercial aircraft manufacturer announced in that it was dropping plans to develop a 550-seat version of its veteran 747 jumbo because it said there was insufficient interest from airlines to justify the $7.0 billion investment envisaged.

In contrast Airbus said last week it believed airlines would need bigger aircraft to meet the rapid growth in demand for air travel over the next 20 years, and vowed to press ahead with plans to get an all-new doubledecker aircraft, the Airbus A3XX, into the air by year 2003 for the same price as an enlarged 747, at around $200 million, at a development cost of $8.0 billion.
Condit was en route to a meeting in Brussels on Tuesday with European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert to discuss EC concerns over Boeing's planned takeover of McDonnell Douglas.

He declined to say what he would tell Van Miert but did not expect that any EC investigation would hold up the timetable for completing the $13 billion deal, but the meeting with Van Miert was likely to be one of several.

"One of the aspects of European regulation is that it does have a timetable...and it's a five-month timetable," he said. "Most of what I want to do (on Tuesday) is listen...dialogue is a two-way proposition."
